title: Navigation for a small consultancy
metaTitle: Navigation for a small consultancy site
excerpt: Label the site as a map of problems, not industries or departments. Use the buyer's words, and keep one path that books a working session.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, a formal facade that can look like an institution rather than a problem.
caption: A grand facade is not a map of the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a small consultancy's main navigation?
faqs.answer: Use the problem, how a session runs, the fee, proof, and a booking. Those match the questions of a buyer comparing you with doing the work themselves. Industry menus and department names can exist only as quieter links, and usually they should not exist at all.

faqs.question: How many header items are enough?
faqs.answer: Five is enough, and one of them should book the working session. A longer bar starts to look like a larger firm's org chart. Do not invent menu children to look scaled. A wrong buyer should be able to tell the problem is not theirs.

faqs.question: How should the menu work on a phone?
faqs.answer: Use the same labels, in the same order, with the booking obvious when the menu opens. Do not depend on hover. Give each item room to tap, and do not hide the only action under a tall image.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small consultancy website navigation is a map of the problems you take, not a list of departments or industries. A buyer comparing you with doing the work themselves should see labels they already use, and one path that books a working session. "About, Services, Industries, Insights, Contact" is an org chart. It tells them you are organized. It does not tell them whether you take their stuck decision.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview organizes the guidelines under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Labels fail the understandable principle when they are private jargon or a row of sectors. A menu fails the operable principle when it depends on a hover. Nielsen Norman Group's research puts a clock on the words: the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and many leave within 10 to 20 seconds. They will not open "Industries" to discover you had a problem in mind.

## Problems, not departments

Name the items the way the buyer names the stuck work. The problem, or the few problems you take. How a session runs. The fee shape. Proof, meaning a decision someone would have delayed. Book a session. That map matches the questions they arrived with. Do you take this problem. What happens in the hour. What does it cost compared with my time. Have you forced this choice before. How do I book.

Department labels answer the staff. Where the essays live. Where the careers page is. Those can exist as quiet links. They should not be the primary row. A buyer who sees "Industries" first will assume there is no problem, only range, and range is the reason they think they can do it themselves. They know their sector. They do not know if you will end the hour with a decision.

Keep the row short. Five items is enough. If you have two problems, they can be two items, or one item called by the shared refusal if the session is the same. Do not invent children to make the menu look like a larger firm. A small firm with a large menu looks like it is performing scale. This buyer is allergic to that performance.

The order is a sentence. Problem, session, fee, proof, book. A person who only reads the bar should be able to reconstruct the offer. If you lead with the firm's story and put the problem third, you have rebuilt the brochure in the navigation.

## Words they already use when they hesitate

Take the labels from the complaint, not from a brand workshop. "Pricing" beats "Commercial excellence." "The session" beats "Our methodology." "Fees" beats "Engagement models." "Book a working session" beats "Get in touch."

Test a label on someone who has the problem and has been solving it alone. If they ask what it means, it is not a label yet. Do not ship the clever word and hope the page explains it. People who leave in the first 10 seconds do not click through for a translation.

Avoid labels any firm could use. "Solutions." "Platform." "Insights." A buyer has clicked those and found essays. Your label should be falsifiable. A wrong buyer should feel this is not their problem. That feeling means the navigation is doing its job.

The current page should be obvious without color alone. WCAG's perceivable principle means information cannot live only in a hue. A bold label, or a page title that repeats the item, survives daylight on a phone. A pale underline does not.

## One path that books the session

One item is the action. "Book a working session." It should go to the same place as the button on the homepage. If the bar says "Contact" and the homepage says "Book a working session," you have two products. Pick the session.

The path should be on proof pages and on the fee page. Someone who has just recognized their own delay should not hunt the footer. Repeat the action. Do not put "Subscribe" beside it at the same weight. A newsletter is not the comparison they came to make.

Leave the navigation visible on the booking page. A trapped form feels like a funnel, and a funnel feels like the sales process they were hoping to avoid by doing the work themselves. Let them leave. The ones who book will have chosen to.

If an offer has its own page, the link there can name the problem. "Book a pricing session." The global item stays broad enough for any problem you actually take. Both must be honest. Neither should open a calendar titled "intro" unless an intro is the offer.

## What does not belong in the bar

Drop an industry menu. It is the homepage failure, repeated on every page. Drop a blog with no tie to the problems. Drop a login, social icons, and a search box on a thin site. The login can live in the footer for clients who already know it. Social icons in the header ask for a detour before the problem is named.

Do not add a large panel of links to avoid choosing words. Twenty links is a second homepage, usually a list of sectors. If you have three problems, list those three. If you have one, the menu can be almost boring. Boring and true is the point.

Footer labels must match the header. An old footer that says "Industries" while the header says "Pricing" reads as neglect. Pick one set of words. The buyer who might do the work themselves is looking for a reason you are less disciplined than they are. A contradictory menu is that reason.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Most of these buyers will open the site on a phone between other work, which is also how they have been failing to make the decision. The menu cannot depend on hover. WCAG applies to mobile, and the operable principle means the items can be reached without a mouse-only gesture. A compact menu is fine if it opens the same five labels, in the same order, with the session still obvious.

Put the booking in the open menu as a button, and consider a persistent control when the menu is closed. Do not bury the only action inside the menu and under a tall image. Give each item enough space to tap. "Book a working session" fits. "Schedule a confidential strategic conversation" does not. The page it opens can carry the longer promise.

Read the open menu aloud. If you run out of breath before the booking, cut an item. The phone is where this buyer will decide whether you are simpler than another month of doing it alone.

## When a partner wants the industries back

The menu will be challenged. A partner will say a buyer in clinics will not click "Pricing" unless they see healthcare. That fear is the industry list trying to return. The answer is not a submenu of sectors. The answer is a problem sentence that already contains the setting when the setting changes the work, on the page itself, not in the bar. The bar stays short. The page can be specific.

If you truly serve two problems that a buyer would never confuse, give them two labels and stop. Do not add the sectors those problems happen to sit in. A clinic pricing problem and a factory pricing problem can share the label "Pricing" if the session and the refusal are the same, and the proof pages can show the settings. The navigation does not need to do the proof's job.

Write the objection down and the reply next to it, so the next redesign does not relitigate it. "We removed industries because a buyer comparing us with doing it themselves reads a sector list as generic. The problem label stays." That note is part of the design. Without it, the menu grows back the week a new page is added, because a new page wants a new item, and a new item wants a parent called Industries.

Also check in-page links. A button in the middle of a proof that says "See our industries" undoes the bar. Search the site for the old labels after you rename them. Leftover anchors are how the org chart survives the redesign. Replace them with the problem, or remove them. A site with two vocabularies is two sites, and the buyer will believe the older, vaguer one.

## A label test this week

Write the labels in a plain list. Show them to three people who have postponed the problem. Ask where they would click to see the problem, the cost, and how to book. If they hesitate, change the word. Do not add a tooltip.

Then count the taps from the homepage to a booked session. More than two means the path is still a department tour. Check the current-page marker on the fee page and on a proof page. Check that the footer does not resurrect an industry list you removed from the header.

When the labels match the problems, the pictures have to match them too. A bar that says "Pricing" under a collage of sectors is a broken map. Read [how to photograph the problem rather than the industries](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-small-consultancy) before the new labels ship on the old imagery.

If you want the map of a site drawn around the work rather than a list of sectors, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The labels are part of the design, not a list added the week of launch.
